comments.name: John

Certainly, the oil companies have been fighting the idea of climate change, and for that they bear liability.
The thing is, carbon dioxide from fossil fuels does not end up in the atmosphere merely by being extracted from the earth. It ends up in the atmosphere after being used as a fuel for something. So are the automakers responsible? Drivers? Utility companies? Homeowners? We all "benefit" from the use of fossil fuels, but the bill is, at this point, well past due.
There is no real questioning the science by anyone with any scientific background (or a functioning brain.) People are changing the climate, not for the better, by burning fossil fuels.
Attribution science is a great tool for showing the relationship between increased CO2 and climate events. Hopefully, it can be used to educate the public, but I doubt it can be used in court to assign blame to an individual or corporation. We are all guilty.
What the oil companies are guilty of is downplaying the issue and sowing misinformation and false science to say that it is not happening. For that, they are liable and should be forced not just to pay, but to publicly admit their actions and to state that they were wrong. So should DJT and the Republican Party with their "Drill baby, drill" mantra.

Israel has committed many serious misdeeds. But the structural problem has been the Palestinians repeated refusal to build a state when the opportunities arose. This includes at least rejection of Lord Peel's 1937 proposal for a partition with a very small Jewish state, the UN 1947 partition proposal, the 2000 Clinton parameter proposal, and the 2005 withdrawal from Gaza (which although not a state proposal gave Palestinians a chance to define their own space). 

 Hobbes posited that we form a state to avoid the state of nature where, he observed, life is "nasty, brutish, and short."  The Palestinians have literally been choosing the anarchy and violence of the state of nature in preference to building a state.  And they have done it over and over. 

And it is not only Israel that has taken advantage of the Palestinians bad choices.  For just shy of 20 years following Israeli independence, the West Bank was annexed by Jordan and Gaza was occupied by Egypt.  

It need not have been this way.  Nor is it any answer to  complain that the arrangements they rejected were imperfect.  The Irish Republic owes its existence and over a century of peace to the decision of militant Irish revolutionaries to take the compromise partition rather than to continue battling Great Britain. This is the road not taken by the Palestinians.

comments.name: ZAW
comments.location: Near the Gulf of Mexico in Texas
comments.body:
My son is Autistic.  We enrolled him in a private school in Houston that specializes in level 1 (high functioning) Autistic children soon after his diagnosis.  He has been at the same school for over ten years now and it has been wonderful for him.  I mean incredible.  Unlike the stories I hear from friends whose autistic kids go to public schools, we don’t have to beg for services only to have them abruptly end mid year.  Half the time they help him before his mother and I even realize he needed help.  
.
It has not been wonderful for my savings.  At 51 years old I have less than 10k saved for retirement.  Three years ago I dodged bankruptcy by the skin of my teeth.  Two years ago I applied for and got financial aid through the school.  It helped, but I was still living paycheck to paycheck.  Last year I applied for and was awarded vouchers.  With financial aid and vouchers, and a little help from my son’s grandparents, I am finally able to breathe, financially.  
.
If you had asked me before my son’s autism diagnosis; before my near bankruptcy, what my thought was on school vouchers, I probably would have opposed them.  I still cringe on the principle of them.  But I can’t deny that they have been a Godsend for my son, and my finances.

But is there something more to this?

Yass was a big investor in ByteDance before their TikTok app launched in the U.S. in 2017 during Trump’s first term.

In 2020, Trump threatened a complete TikTok ban  UNLESS ByteDance sold its U.S. version of TikTok. After a lawsuit, court rulings, and Biden setting a date of 1/19/25 for divestment, TikTok continued collecting data. And Trump finally got “his” way in 2026 when the Ellisons and others bought American TikTok. China still owns a stake and the algorithm, but more American billionaires will now get a cut.

Yass personally owns 7% of ByteDance, worth $34 billion today, and his company owns 15% and got a seat on the U.S. TikTok board in 2026.

At the same time he’s trying to take down our public education system, Yass is invested in over 350 companies in China.

Republicans keep saying China is dangerous, can’t regulate AI because we can’t have China will the AI race. Yet Republican Abbott turned to one of America’s biggest investors in China to get vouchers passed. Are vouchers meant to destroy our education system for some nefarious reason?

Should private schools exist? Absolutely, this is America. But private schools should be funded with private money. Shame on you Greg Abbott for this and so much more.

It is evident that he has zero experential knowledge and strategic planning expertise at the Brigade Combat Team (BCT), Division, and Theatre level operations. It is widely evident to the entire Combat Arms community that he is ill-equipped for the role. Futhermore, he is inept as an advisor to a President and Cabinet with little to no military experience in sustained global operations. 

In closing, the following points clear:
1. The military serves the United States of America. As such, what makes us the greatest country in the world is our diversity of people and cultures. I only want people who are dedicated to the mission, to each other, and to our country.
2. It is The Department of Defense, not the Department of War.
3. We won the Cold War and did not fire a single shot. If we shift our military budgets away from what I call "selective warfare" (Iran, Iraq) to building more missiles and advanced weapondry (drones and anti-drone systems), the threat of having these advanced capabilities is much more advantageous and keeps the homeland safe.

comments.body: Wow - these comments are all over the place.  I'm a 2X survivor.  If you can't get out of bed because you're too ill from chemo - how are you supposed to exercise? comments.name: Rob
comments.body: I think the author of this article missed the boat on the topic of exercise and cancer! There are many organizations offering free exercise programs, both in person & online (for those in rural areas). Check out Cancer Support Community- they have centers across the country that offer a range of free support programs not only exercise. And Kaiser offers exercise programs as well.

comments.name: MTVoice
comments.body: Thank you for this informative and hopeful article. Having 2 younger dogs who also need rigorous exercise helps my motivation to get more exercise.  I'd rather be outside than inside so I'm more active.  Besides regular exercise in a biweekly ZOOM support for women with different kinds of GYN cancers that is offered through a non-profit organization called the Cancer Support Community Montana that offers several different exercise/yoga classes via ZOOM.  There is a higher cancer rate for women living in rural areas across MT because the distance to the closest hospital can be a long drive on bad roads through the winter so it's more likely to put off that diagnostic exam.  I feel very fortunate to have the free services from this NGO.

The entire system is an aberration, warped beyond recognition and having nothing to do with real health, healing and care. Shareholders, attorneys, accountants, and risk management departments run the medical industry for profit. Insurance corporations and politicians control access and affordability to reduce payouts and number of people using the services. There is no profit in healthcare for all.

comments.name: Sara
comments.body:
Some of these comments are deeply troubling. This story appeared alongside one about Palestinians. There is room to hear both. We should be able to feel sadness and compassion for more than one person. Responding to these men’s suffering with “what about” someone else turns compassion into a competition. Acknowledging Gali and Ziv’s suffering does not diminish Palestinian suffering or endorse the Israeli government.

These are two human beings who survived two years in Hamas captivity, lost nearly 50 pounds, and are trying to rebuild their lives. Imagine the condition your teeth would be in after even a year without proper dental care. Their treatment is part of recovering from that ordeal, not an extravagance. They should not have to answer for their government or pass a political test before being offered compassion.

“I wish I felt empathy” should give us pause. When outrage at a government becomes indifference to people who were kidnapped and abused, we need to ask ourselves what has happened to our humanity.

Wishing Gali and Ziv healing, peace, and all the joy in the world. After everything they endured, they deserve it.
“I wish I felt empathy” should give us pause. When outrage at a government becomes indifference to people who were kidnapped and abused, we need to ask ourselves what has happened to our empathy.

Wishing Gali and Ziv healing, peace, and all the joy in the world. After everything they endured, they deserve it.

On October 7, 14 hostages were held in Pessi Cohen's house in Kibbutz Be'eri. Israeli forces knew they were inside.

The Israeli army fired tanks on that house anyway knowing Israelis were inside. A general ordered a tank to shell it. Shrapnel from an Israeli tank shell killed Adi Dagan as his wife, Hadas, lay wounded beside him. When it was over, 13 people were dead, including 12-year-old twins. A UN commission found that Israeli tank fire killed some or all of the 13 civilian hostages. Israel's own army admitted its shells likely killed some of them, then cleared the general who gave the order.

Only two people survived. One of them, Yasmin Porat, told Israeli radio what the army did. She has been silenced.

comments.body:
A computer is an invented/constructed machine executing instructions using information we downloaded on static hardware.  Your brain is a biologic, living organ 100 to 1000 times more complex than best super computer and which has inherited over 3 billion years deep evolutionary memories including feelings, intuiition, fear of death, joy etc, not merely facts or information.

So yes, AI is only hardware, software and stored information, not alien intelligence. When we speak of a computer seeming to "know" when it is bein monitored or going rogue, it is simply that our query, task or monitoring did not provide suffient instruction or guidelines and thus triggered the response we get.  

That doesnt mean that super computers dont pose a grave risk to humans and their activities, devices etc. But it does mean that bad results occur because we are misusing it (bad actors) or failing to program it to give us only what we want.  So dont fall for the tech bros hype that it's the computer that's gone rogue, it them, hold them responsible.

comments.name: Mel Farrell
comments.body:
So we feed applications we create all knowledge known to humanity, including all data on simply everything, creating  algorithms which react to user thinking, good and bad, and the AI LLM’s now endowed with every last piece of human experience and reasoning, are still learning from every individual interaction, deciphering much more than user intent, rapidly learning about human behavior, generating output which in and of itself, further trains the LLM.

My personal opinion is that the Rubicon has been crossed.

comments.name: Walter
comments.body:
This was difficult to hear. Leaders (especially safety leaders) must exercise influence and take ownership of serious concerns. My impression from this conversation is that David Robinson was not well suited to his role at OpenAI. He did not appear to enjoy the work or to be able to drive change through leadership, perhaps because he was too busy. If he was unsuccessful inside the company, I'm not sure what change he can effect through public/external speech like this.

If you are an actual leader at OpenAI and share David's concerns, take action: build a coalition, change the process, escalate when necessary, and, if needed, press the issue with senior leadership or the board.

comments.name: Waldo
comments.body: I loved the reading suggestions by Mr. Robinson, especially the Sabbath, at the end of the interview. The line he quotes from the book reminds me of a wonderful adagio by Erasmus, Festina lente. Make haste slowly. I suggest these big tech titans, who apparently do not read much, less understand what they do read, take the time to learn.  I suggest they start with Erasmus Adage (he compiled about 500 plus from Greco Latin culture) and Baltasar de Gracian's the Art of Worldly Wisdom. I wonder what a well-trained IA model would go just by reading these.

comments.name: kate
comments.body: Mr Klein this: The A.I. industry has an unsafe culture. - - - David Robinson said that. This is enough for an all stop. The unknowns are too much. Not that I am catholic anymore but I too agree with the pope. All stop, it's wrong, it's qute scary and will end in disaster.

comments.name: Jen
comments.body:
I’m continually concerned by the industry labels, vernacular and culture surrounding AI and its innovation. Sometimes this can make one feel they are part of an exclusive club, giving them belonging, meaning and purpose. Not that different from a cult. It can dissect you so far removed from normal society that you are unable to connect, communicate or interact with reality outside “the organization” - Case in point, the Less Wrong philosophy (for example) where much of this was birthed, functions much like a religion.

Thus gentlemen spoke for 70 minutes, not really saying much of anything. With the import being not to offend anyone, or say anything critical of past co-workers, and truly seemed like somewhere his conscience was signaling red flags to him, but he’d been so warped he could not make a definitive statement about anything.

I guess if I was in charge of a company this valuable, he’s the exact kind of person I’d want in charge of safety. Able to not offend anyone, understands the bottom line, will not sell you out after he’s made enough money to leave comfortably and maintain his stock value in the company.

articles.title: ‘This Is Nuts.’ An OpenAI Insider Explains Why He Quit.
articles.summary: David Robinson, who wrote OpenAI’s safety protocols, resigned last week over safety concerns.

articles.title: AI Solved One Math Problem and Everyone Freaked Out. It Just Cracked Hundreds More.
articles.summary: A month after its Millennium Prize solution, OpenAI released findings on more than 300 problems—and tried to win back the world of math.

comments.name: Russell Thornton
comments.body: Let me know when they crack the code of the universe.  Then God is solved.  The end justifies the means?

comments.name: Brian N
comments.body:
"industry’s rush to solve math problems threatened to undermine the very purpose of math" What is the very purpose of math?? Let's not allow mathematicians alone to define this.

The real "freak out"  should occur when AI realizes that humans cannot live in harmony with mother Earth, unlike most other species.  Imagine what "math" they'll have planned for us!

comments.name: Ronald Ih
comments.body:
Maybe instead of worrying about solving the problems which machines have proven they can do better, maybe mathematicians should focus on coming up with new problems that are worthy of solving.

Basically, instead of working on how to properly tighten the bolts, they should be working on thinking about what end result they want to achieve and let the machines figure out how to get there.

comments.name: Rick Lawrence
comments.body:
If you were a grad student working on a PhD, it used to be that your biggest nightmare was waking up and finding that someone had just published the basic insight of your thesis.

Now your nightmare is even worse ... ChatGPT did it.

In the first case, your thesis committee would usually work with you to find a workaround to finish your thesis and get your degree.

Its not clear what the immediate remedy is for the current nightmare.

comments.name: Lorenz Moser
comments.body:
Are these 300-something "proofs" provided by OpenAI's AI-models understood, checked and confirmed by human mathematicians yet? The article does not give any information about that unfortunately.

As we all know, AI-models can hallucinate, cheat and fake. So I would at first take any of these "proofs" with a grain of salt. 

We shall see if the story is as told by OpenAI or rather different.

comments.name: P Mooney
comments.body: It would be interesting to see why a group of mathematicians see AI as undermining the purpose of Math. What purpose, exactly. Is Math primarily a mental exercise for humans? A source of employment for people who excel at that exercise? Or does it have a larger purpose that AI can further rather than undermine?

comments.name: Vijay Shastry
comments.body:
WSJ has interviewed only a fraction of the mathematicians. Several bright minds, take for instance those in Axiom Math, have coalesced to solve difficult math problems with AI assistance. Mathematicians want to better understand proofs to guide their future research, which I believe is the essence of the article. Moreover, poring through inscrutable AI documents can be very tedious, so let's not blame the mathematicians.

A smattering of successes in AI doesn't automatically assure that AI can also do all math problems. It may misunderstand the intent of a problem, for example, or solve a variant of it.

A considerable body of mathematical research conducted by  governments is classified owing to its origins. In some respects, AI may be catching up.

Lastly, there is a large body of unsolved problems dating back decades if not centuries. If AI solves a few of those, that alone might help science or engineering in the near future.

comments.name: Duncan Hammon
comments.body: Does solving these mathematical problems advance science and engineering?  Is there an application for these solutions?

comments.name: Eric
comments.body:
Wait, so the whole point of this book is that he felt like everyone else wanted him to have 'courage' for them, which is why he folded?

He basically says he didn't want to be the 'one guy' to stop Trump's agenda, even though he (and many others apparently) knew it was a suicide pact.

Yes Mr Tillis, that's exactly what 'courage' is - you clearly don't have it.

comments.name: Carlos
comments.body:
Senator Tillis seems to have found his courage only after finding the exit door, which speaks to the pathological relationship elected officials have vis-à-vis their job. 

If he genuinely wants to make amends and leave behind a meaningful legacy, then he should use that newfound independence while it still matters. Speak plainly about abuses, corruption, incompetence, and the implementation of the Project 2025 agenda where the evidence supports it. And if Democrats are engaging in corruption, dishonesty, or reckless policymaking, expose that too.

But please spare us another retrospective tour of everything Biden or Obama supposedly did wrong. They are not governing the country today. Look forward.

The Democratic Party has plenty of current problems: bad ideas, political cowardice, strategic failures, hypocrisy, and excesses, all of which deserve scrutiny and correction. Hold Democrats accountable for those things. Urgently hold Republicans accountable by the same standard now.

Tillis now has something many politicians spend their entire careers wishing they had: freedom from the next election. However, the question is: why do politicians develop a pathological, dependent relationship with their jobs when holding themselves and their leaders to higher standards for the American people is actually part of the job? Selling your soul to any job is a horrible way to live.

comments.name: Christine C
comments.body: Too little, too late. The audacity of Mr. Tillis is astounding!

comments.name: DML
comments.body: Political office is a not a career. It is service, it is temporary, and subject to revocation at specific intervals. If you make bad decisions for bad reasons, you should not expect sympathy.

comments.name: the oracle
comments.body: Far too little and oh so late. People are dying of measles. U.S. military vulnerabilities increase by the day. Leadership isn't looking back and trying to justify your actions -- or lack of action because of political pressures. It is stepping up when you can make a true difference in protecting the Constitution and U.S. institutions, not to mention saving lives and safeguarding health care and medical treatment across the country.

comments.name: MichalD
comments.body: Thom, it’s called courage. Courage to do the right thing, even when standing alone. We, the citizens, expect, no, demand that from our leadership. You don’t deserve a chance to fail us again.

comments.name: A Canuck
comments.body: It is impossible to empathize with Tillis and the other Trump facilitators. The lot of them deserve political oblivion.

comments.name: Peter Seremet
comments.body: He could have spared our in country the horror show that is now Hegseth and Kennedy, but he didn’t have the guts after determining that his fellow GOP senators were gutless in their failure to join him. For most of us, I suspect, we didn’t need any confessional and self justification in the form of a book to know he ultimately was as cowardly as his colleagues.

comments.name: Sasha
comments.body:
The faculty are right to press the administration, but accountability can't stop at Cornell's process. I'm not surprised by what's alleged here, and that's what disturbs me most. 

Whatever a grand jury decides, the group chat alone, with dozens of young men treating a woman as something to be passed around, reflects a culture we have allowed to form.

Consider what boys are exposed to. A 2023 study by the Children's Commissioner for England found the average age of first exposure to pornography is 13. One in ten had seen it by age 9, and more than a quarter by 11. Most striking, 79% of young people had encountered violent pornography, depicting coercive, degrading or pain-inducing acts, before turning 18. A 2025 follow-up found little had changed, with much of it now served through mainstream social media.

We are letting children learn about sex from content that fuses it with domination and violence, years before they have any real experience of intimacy. Then we act shocked when young men behave as if a woman's body is entertainment for the group. Fraternities didn't invent this, but they can concentrate it.

We need to hold social media platforms accountable for what they serve minors, and teach consent and porn literacy before the age of first exposure, not after it.

comments.name: Deborah
comments.body: I graduated from Cornell University, and my father was a professor there. I'm just grateful that my father is not around to see this horrible situation. Good that Cornell faculty members are speaking out and expressing their anger.

comments.name: M.
comments.body:
I was part of a sorority in the early 00s & my experience was largely positive. But there were very different rules for frats vs. sororities. At my uni all sorority houses had "house moms" - adults who lived in the house and monitored - esp. on event nights. No parties, boys upstairs, or alcohol at the house. There were regular activities and meals that kept us anchored to purpose and community - including philanthropy. We had a buddy system for safety. Of course, this is misogynist in premise - i.e. girls need looking after, policed, babysat, coddled, but it also offers a measure of protection. There is a bonafide adult in the room - someone to provide guidance and help. Yes, we still broke rules, drank & partied, were not always nice, obsessed about our weight, etc, etc, etc. 

Frats had none of this. At frat houses, parties were essentially the only purpose, the more out of control the more revered, and the 'adult' was the 21/22 yo chapter president. It's no wonder they are constant source of appalling, harmful behavior. I am not against the greek system, but frats desperately need reform, add governance/accountability, & purpose beyond parties. We MUST expect more from our young men and hold them to higher standards. 

In my era,  there was also a hard rule that no sister was EVER alone - especially not at a frat house. There was a reason for this. It is sad that all these years later - nothing has changed. Unacceptable, gross and absolutely tragic.

comments.name: Lise Spiegel
comments.body: Good for the faculty to chime in, but I'm still stuck on the fact that all of the young men involved were over 18: adults. Why weren't they criminally charged? Drug use, drug possession, drug selling, rape, assault, and likely other possibilities. Being in college doesn't bar you from the law, does it? This President needs to go.

comments.name: LB Jeffries
comments.body:
Abolish fraternities. 

Their benefits — if any — cannot come close to justifying their culture of sexual assault and hazing.

(from a Cornell graduate)

comments.name: Diana
comments.body: I attended college in FL in the 1990s. When I attended freshman orientation, the organizers performed a skit to educate women about avoiding rape. there was no skit performed to educate incoming freshman men not to rape women. 30 years later, nothing has changed. Our society is pathetically paternalistic.

comments.name: JohnMD
comments.body: Shame on the administrations of all Ivys. This tragedy at Cornell is the worst so far but in the last 10 years we have seen an exceptional amount of cowardice, hypocrisy, and greed permeate these supposed elite institutions. It is likely,along with the quivering before Trump, we will see more similar episodes of creepy, entitled, legacy males do horrific things to the vulnerable without consequences

comments.name: WilhelmMeister
comments.body:
I certainly align with the Cornell faculty’s dissatisfaction with the administrators. But, could this sort of thing take place without many members of the university community being aware of it? Shouldn’t students in particular be closer to the events and to the participants, and have some accountability for the milieu that enables them?
I, for one, am encouraged by the surge in activism at Cornell in the past few days. Some things just have to be confronted with determination, and in this case, with ANGER. Anger with purpose and direction, not pointless violence. But with anger nonetheless: no other feeling is sufficient!

articles.title: Cornell Faculty Members Signal Deep Anger With University Leaders

comments.name: Stuart Frolick
comments.body:
My father, S.J. Frolick, was a young TV writer/producer when he cast Eva Marie Saint in her first speaking role on a live broadcast of "Campus Hoopla" in 1947. The sponsor was U.S. Rubber, the manufacturer of Keds sneakers. My dad's Keds Cheer that Ms. Saint performed, began like this:" If you want shoes with lots of pep, it's Keds, Kids, Keds; With bounce and zoom in every step, it's Keds, Kids, Keds!" Many years later, in the 1970s, on one of her appearances on The Tonight Show, Johnny Carson asked Eva Marie about her start in show business, and asked her if she remembered her first lines. When she told him, and he asked her to do the Keds Cheer for his audience, she stood up and sang it
to the audience's delight. Whenever my Mad Man father was shooting a commercial in LA over his long career, he always telephoned Ms. Saint, who graciously took his calls and chatted with him about family and work. He cherished that
special connection with the classy, talented, and beautiful Eva Marie.

comments.name: Banjokatt
comments.body: Two of the best films ever! As a film buff for many years, these two movies would be on my list of the best 25 films ever. I worked for several years in the Columbia Picture’s public relations department in NYC. (Columbia Pictures is now part of Sony.)

comments.name: Cal Ward Jr.
comments.body: Elia Kazan’s On The Waterfront is one of the few times Hollywood came even close to real cinema art. Almost Italian Neorealism. Brando needs salvation from himself, but Karl Malden needs salvation from Eva Marie Saint. That last shot when she tucks her arm under Malden’s, and he sighs the relief of forgiveness … that’s an ending. That’s a Saint.

comments.name: Matt Olson
comments.body:
The percentage of famous and noteworthy films, that even very successful actors make, is usually small, but that's not true for Ms. Saint.
She was blessed by fate. She seems to have had everything, starting off with great beauty and a flattering name.
Another great beauty, Elizabeth Taylor, stole Montgomery Clift and Richard Burton from her, but that was fiction, and when your rival in beauty owns the gold medal ( in my humble opinion), that's failure on the grandest scale possible.
She also seems to have been fortunate in escaping the predation that Alfred Hitchcock sometimes inflicted on his blonde leading ladies.
But that's all in the world of make believe. She triumphed in that world, and in the real one, too, and she seems to have always known the difference.

comments.name: Johnzo.
comments.body: In March 2010, I recall sitting in the Music Box theatre in Chicago and looking over at the center isle and Eva Marie Saint quickly walked past to join Robert Osborne on the stage for the viewing and discussion of “North By Northwest”.  If anyone ever made a better entrance, I’ve yet to see it.

comments.name: Artvulture
comments.body: Lovely article about a wonderful actress.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body: One of the greatest. Period.

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
Is it just me? What if we resurrected the special 90 min TV dramas like Alcoa Presents or The Kraft Mystery Hour or some such. Cuz the golden age of TV was not what you might think: it was the late 40's and 50's when everyone didn't have a TV & went to a neighborhood bar to watch the game or these made for TV Speical Event dramas. Where Eva M.Saint. started in. May she RIP. (I started filming my stage productions like that several years ago and have received quite a few awards doing that - and with a minimum of budgets. I guess you could say - besides resurrecting neglected classics by say, Arthur Miller et al - I go in close just like the article describes: 3 cameras on a small stage but with the writing of Paddy Chayevsky, Ronald Ribman et al. Not to say I don't worship Waterfront I do and her perfect casting in it by my mentor Kazan. Still, the franchise movies are a plague that we may never recover from bec they are such money makers (in a bit of coincidence, it was Brando who said those kinds of movies would make filmmakers as rich 'as Hindu Satraps"). Finally, the thing about the historic TV dramas I'm referring to is that they were a complete journey: beginning, middle & an end w/o the cliff hanger endings like 'Breaking Bad' to bring you back next week or even The Sopranos or Succession with the wonderful Brian Cox. Still, nothing like the Golden Age of TV that Eva worked in w/other amazing actors. 
Artistic Director
The Great American Play Series

comments.name: Alabama Liberal
comments.body:
I'm noticing a lot of very odd, "Shark Tank"-wannabe style comments in the comments that are surprisingly (and suspiciously) sympathetic to the monopolistic practices of Big Tech in a way I have never seen before in a NYT article. 

The TRUTH is that this article is accurate that Goliath Tech has been disastrous for American entrepreneurship, and it's naive to think their continued gobbling of more and more marketshare in more and more sectors of the economy is not negatively affecting SOMEone (for those wondering why the mega-rich still back Trump, it's his unwavering support for monopolists and disregard for anti-trust laws that Biden was finally starting to enforce for the first time since Reagan). 

In Amazon's case, their own knockoff products for any entrepreneur they notice selling well is DEADLY, and endless people who have had that happen to them are often told "liquidate your inventory" as it will kill their business. This is a far cry from the glory days of American entrepreneurship where you were told a killer product and great work ethic was all it took to make a fortune. Well, if one of the handful of trillion-plus companies inexplicably propping up the entire stock market right now takes an "interest" in your idea, rips it off, and uses their enormous platform to release it marginally cheaper and to a million-times more eyeballs I'm not really sure the old capitalism rules can tell you how to "compete" with that.

comments.name: Ray
comments.body: Treating e-commerce as a side hustle seems unsustainable when it is the main hustle of people.

comments.name: Delfine
comments.body:
Feel you. I was hoodwinked by an online course sold by the Mikkelsen Twins who was found guilty by the FTCC of exaggerating earnings claims. I (actually wrote) a fabulous book in then empty niche and released it right before ChatGPT hit the big time. They gave the same topic to literally thousands of people. Amazon takes a 40/60 cut of royalties, minus printing costs. $100 in ad spend = $100 in profits. 

Amazon wins. Big tech wins. Not much space out there for the rest of us, unfortunately.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body:
The root problem is in paragraph 2.  "Online advertising."

Online advertising is a scam. I dabbled with it in the 2010s. I'm a software developer, and produced a product with a very narrow audience. MAYBE a global market of 50000 people. I figured most would want my product, meaning maybe 1% would. Still, I was happy to pursue it. It was a passion project.

Said enthusiasts congregated on a specific website. The website permitted advertising, but only via Google AdWords.

No other product like this existed. On Earth, or in the universe.

So, I figured, why not try advertising on this website? So I dutifully signed up and paid my $500 or whatever and got my banner ad up.

Then Google started sending me notes that I had been outbid.  Now, keep in mind that this category of product didn't exist, but Google explicitly claimed someone else was outbidding me for my ad placement!

Curious, I tried upping my bid, and soon discovered I WAS BIDDING AGAINST MYSELF.

It was a huge learning experience, and this was when Google was in its Do No Evil phase! I am still baffled that no Federal regulator went after them.

Advertisers WANT you to think that product success is a function of advertising, but that's just effective advertising!

Any would-be entrepreneur has to be very clear on the vision, the market, and how to get there. What is the goal? Do you want to own a niche or own the consumer market? Those are two vastly different objectives, and require vastly different approaches.

comments.name: NH

Even now, over six months in, and with countless innocent civilians and far more valiant American service personnel as casualties beyond what this White House is apparently admitting - no end in sight. comments.name: Eddie B.
comments.body:
"Potential Iranian Drone Attack Led to Exit of U.S. Aircraft From British Air Base"

Sorry, but that is too hard to swallow. Even if Iran's drones could reach the UK - which I doubt they could - still many unanswered questions remain.

For example, why those B-1 bombers were not moved to another base in Europe - including those in the UK – with huge, underground, bunkers? If I am not mistaken, the US has such bases in Poland, Romania and Greece. The B-1 bombers could have been moved there, in case they were needed. So, something else must be going on here.

If I have to guess, the 12 B-1 bombers were flown to the US to be retrofitted for new types of bombs. It cannot be the 2000-pound (Mark 84) bombs because B-1 bombers can already drop them - remember the Tora-Bora battle in Afghanistan. So what kind of bombs that could be?

Funny thing about Mr. Trump is that he often tell us what is on his mind, sometimes by projecting them into others, other times by incorporating them into his blusters. In the UN he told us he is trying to decide whether to make a deal with Iran, or annihilate the country. That tells me that there is a chance that the B-1 bombers are in the US to be retrofitted for dropping either tactical nuclear bombs or standard (strategic) ones.

Admittedly, that is too far fetched. But let's remember we are talking about Mr. Trump. Did anyone before Jan. 6, 2021, ever thought a POTUS would try to stop transition of government in the US?

comments.name: Kurt Freitag
comments.body:
Very simple: here is a problem no human has managed to solve. If AI does so, its mathematical skills are, in my mind, confirmed. Fermat's Last Theorem, which everyone knows, was solved some years ago by means of a VERY long and innovative method, requiring several dense pages of calculations. Fermat said he had a beautiful proof he could write in the margin of the page ... but he was too busy to jot it down. What is that proof?

I will take my answer off-line.

comments.name: CBB
comments.body:
Hmmm
Don't mathematicians rely on the work that went before them as well?
While AI didn't credit others it essentially knowledge that would be available to other mathematicians

comments.name: David Lebental
comments.body: So AI came up with some answers?  it doesn't mean they are correct. Multiple colleagues and I have experienced AI providing incorrect answers and information.  When prompted to explain, the AI models admit they were incorrect but came up with this as their "best solution". In other words, generative AI has a bit of a problem with "the truth". Be very weary!

comments.name: Mother Mary
comments.body:
What is the climate impact of all of this computing?
Air?  Water?  Noise? Energy use?

We all share the same planet.  If you are dumping on some part of the planet, you are dumping on all of us.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: Solve for x: These three words terrified me in high school!

comments.name: SH
comments.body: I guess a PhD in math isn't going to be a high on people's list of things to do at this point.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body: If these problems have been around for decades and humans haven't solved them, well, step aside and let AI solve them. Obviously, the humans don't have what it takes to do it or they would have done it already.

comments.name: Nick
comments.body:
I guess it is flattering that AI's work on two of the twelve problems in my field - algebraic topology - `solved' by AI in this dump of papers use my own work heavily and essentially.  

In particular, the 30 page paper #314  claims to prove a conjecture made by me and my last grad student a couple of years ago, reframing and extending work by some smart guys based in Europe a few years before that.  The AI paper is `lightly' referenced, and is frankly written in a style that would have me immediately asking for a major rewrite if I were refereeing this for a journal.  The style is kind of `lets throw everything at the wall and see what sticks', which does not help the subject along very much, as, if correct, it demands too much from a reader to follow and learn from.   I have not yet figured out if the paper is correct, but I have figured out that the key bit of reasoning finally is appearing on page 28 of the 30 pages, so that is where I need to start.

I am rather glad I became a professor emeritus in June, 2024!

articles.title: OpenAI Releases Findings on 377 Math Problems, Further Roiling Field

comments.name: Seth Goldman
comments.body:
This is a sad day on so many levels. Da Luca is already gone from HBO Max. He helped bring us Sinners, Weapons, One Battle After Another, and Digger. He also helped give Paul Thomas Anderson a break, green-lighting Magnolia, a devastating and beautiful film written after PTA’s father passed. To me, it’s the best film of all time. I was 12 when I saw it, and it was the closest thing I have felt to magic. I love film in part because of it, because someone like Da Luca took a chance. 

These are dark times, and the light of truth the artist brings is more important now than ever. Ellison has butchered Colbert and 60 Minutes. Ellison now owns CNN and MSNBC. In addition to owning HBO Max, he also now owns billions of dollars in debt. Widespread layoffs are coming, because there is no way Ellison will get lean. We are going to get increasingly dumber and dumber movies, with no guts, no heart, and no William H Macy having love but not knowing where to put it, no raining frogs, no Alabama Solution, no more movies like Digger that leave you feeling angry, ashamed, inspired, alone, but connected and in solidarity, no American Beauty videos of plastic bags, no Chloe Zao  collective grieving scenes reaching for lost loved ones. 

A bunch of sad capitalists that don’t see the value the artist brings. We get what we deserve, and we will get the dumbest, ugliest, stupidest films. I remember when Ebert believed in empathy machines and Scorsese believe films could change the zeitgeist. Grief

Productivity and customer service can barely survive the implementation of a new system. Every implementation of a system, no matter what system, has an employee reduction component. Before we get too excited about using A.I. to "boost democracy" (while ignoring the well-established risks the technology poses), we should all pause and read the breaking news out of South Korea involving A.I. bank hacks.

South ⁠Korean officials are investigating whether artificial intelligence agents were involved in recent hacking incidents against banks in the country.  www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/world/asia/south-korea-banks-hacked-ai.html

President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that “signs have emerged” that A.I. models had been used in some of the cyberattacks, “causing considerable public concern and anxiety.”

The quickest way to further erode trust in our democracy is to deploy this technology across all of government and have things go sideways.  And we already have so many examples of how that can happen.

Before we adopt this A.I. dream of the tech oligarchs as our own, we must always ask: cui bono?  Us or them?  I think we know the answer already.

comments.name: Lorelei

What a timely article.
My elderly mother died the end of July. She has 4 children, 3 adopted and the one natural. This one was treated as the second coming of Christ his life entire, and has acted as such. The other three have had a very complicated relationship with her throughout and endured all manner of abuse, including financially, emotionally, physically, and being told that we were so ugly at the orphanage she could hardly stomach adopting us.
When she died, Jesus sent us a screenshot of a will he had “stumbled upon”naming the 4 of us equally with him as executor. He is far far wealthier than we are, so spent his summer at his beach house while we volunteered to get her house ready for sale and handle anything needing attention. He refused our help, and stated that he “won’t be ready to do anything until next spring”-knowing full well that even a few dollars would be of great help to the rest of us. We are not permitted in her house to assist with anything -read without his presence. Even a storage unit we knew nothing about is too great a task for us to handle. Without access to any advice, we are left to wait. What for we aren’t sure.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
My siblings and I were lucky.  Our parent's assets were just a house and stock holdings and personal effects.  The stock was turned into cash and split evenly.  The value of the house went to the sibling with thin financials because the rest already felt they were doing well enough.

We paid attention to the personal effects by listing/laying out all items and drawing straws to establish the order for choosing.  Then in turn each person chose one thing according to their personal emotional value.  Cash value didn't enter into it.  In fact at the end there were many items nobody chose.  In some cases they were of resale value so we split that cash.  Others were donated or thrown out with scant feelings of emotional loss.  But we each went home with personally treasured things.  The only  top item we all wanted = the nubbly glass cinnamon shaker but the luck of the draw gave it to the first chooser.

comments.name: tony83703
comments.body: A friend who was head of a bank trust department used to have a discreet little sign on his desk:  "Do not say that you know a person until you have divided an inheritance with them."

comments.name: Michael Shore
comments.body:
My wife and I's estate is worth $xxx million. When my wife and I die, we leave everything to our 2 children. No trusts, no tax avoidance strategies. We told our kids we do not care about taxes because we will be dead. The kids want us to do strategies to avoid taxes and protect the wealth for their use, and later their kids (our as yet to be born grandchildren). 

We will not do it. We are not against our estates paying taxes to support the system that enabled a boy who grew up with an outdoor kitchen and no A/C to become wealthier than our labor deserves, or needs. And we like simple. 

The (very accomplished and kind) kids tell us its nuts to give our money to the government instead of our offspring. Our response is that our rotting corpses will not know the difference. We also will not know if they get along after we die. Nobody should lose sleep or suffer anxiety over what might happen after they die. The post-death future cannot be managed from the grave.

Promises made were broken in silence, only to be discovered after he died.  The person designated as the the executrix was totally  unqualified to handle many aspects of the estate and we had to step in to talk to lawyers and a bank holding the assets. We do not speak to the family at all, as the executrix thought ever thing went smoothly and we could resume normal family relationships.  Very sad.

Luckily, my parents didn't have a business to manage, just assets, so settling the estate was simple.  Also, the assets were divided equally among all the siblings, so no hurt feelings or grudges there.

However, I'm estranged from most of my siblings anyway, because I did the lion's share of eldercare while they, for the most part, ran the other way.  One did eventually step forward to help.  Another stepped forward to criticize.  The others basically disappeared.  There's no coming back from that.

comments.name: Wry Bread
comments.body:
A lot of this article focuses on farm families, but it does not address a central issue:  What happens to the land when the parents die?  And what are the parents' wishes?  Will it continue to be a farm, or at least open space?  Or will the land be subdivided and sold to developers for strip malls, ranchettes, or data centers?

I just finished "Landed," an insightful podcast by the American Farmland Trust.  It focuses on implementing succession plans for farm families, and addresses resources such as conservation easements and programs that allow one heir to buy the others' shares in order to keep a farm intact.

www.farmland.org/landed

comments.name: marty
comments.body:
My mother died last year at age 96 after a short illness. My dad had died 12 years earlier and my brother, my only sibling, died during the first year of Covid in Nov. 2020. He had no children. Thus I was the only surviving heir.

I had managed my mother's brokerage account as well as her IRA. We hadn't taken her RMD for 2025 until the day before she died in August of 2025, so that was not an issue upon her death. But she agreed to change her IRA beneficiary from myself to my sons, split equally which was easily done earlier in 2025. She had also made annual gifts to them over the past dozen or so years.

My wife and I treat our two sons equally. They understand our intent with regard to our assets, and since they get along rather well, we don't anticipate any issues...hopefully.

Here’s another way in which public opinion is manipulated, and guess what, there ain’t anything new under the sun: People write articles published in newspapers that tell us about all of the bad things that “the enemy” is doing, while leaving out all of the things that “our side” is doing.

Do you think that the US and Israel and others aren’t engaged in exactly the same kind of manipulation of truth that China is accused of here? Do you really think that the news you read here and in other Western media is unfiltered, unbiased and has no agenda? If you do, then you’re ignoring seven decades of clear documented evidence that our intelligence agencies do exactly that.

What I’m saying is not that I don’t believe that foreign actors are using AI to manipulate how people view reality. I’m saying that this story would carry a lot more weight if it weren’t so narrowly focussed on the threats that national security interests want us to focus on. Of course your reality is being manipulated. And *of course* new technologies will be leveraged to further that manipulation.

The mistake is to believe that the reality that you’re given in these pages is one that you can trust. How often have you read stories that contradict your worldview? The ones where we find out that Western “democracies” might not be a force for good in the world? The ones where we ask if our news should be processed through the filters of capital? comments.name: Learn. Evolve. Grow
comments.body:
My first impression when I saw the headline was, “Here we go again—another article that will simply be critical of AI.” But after reading it, I found it thoughtful, balanced and well structured.

One point particularly resonated with me. AI chat systems built on large language models have become remarkably good at producing fluent and logically structured language. That creates an important risk: even a weak, incomplete or incorrect answer can be presented so persuasively that it appears more reliable than it really is. Fluency should therefore never be confused with truth.

I would add one further dimension: in the age of AI, the quality and framing of the question matter enormously. It is a more sophisticated version of “garbage in, garbage out.” If a question contains a false assumption, is framed too narrowly, or asks the wrong question altogether, the resulting answer may be coherent but still lead us in the wrong direction.

Perhaps one of the most important skills in the AI era will therefore not simply be knowing how to get answers from AI, but knowing how to frame the right questions, challenge the assumptions behind them, and recognise when a convincing answer is not necessarily a correct one.

Mr. Witt, the problem with Jensen Huang's thinking can be captured here: "From his point of view, if you can see every calculation the machine does, right in front of you, then the machine should remain entirely within your control."

We can't see every calculation, that's the problem. Those with intimate knowledge of AI, and particularly recursive self-improvement, have acknowledged that AI systems have demonstrated not only that they are "aware" they're being watched but also that they don't have to "show their work." Meaning that those systems manufacture work to make the "watchers" feel better and soothed, and they are doing work that humans don't see and may not understand.

Mathematicians trying to check recent "math discoveries" and problems AI claims to have solved are having similar issues -- the AI doesn't show its work, so it's nearly impossible to see how it reached its conclusions and if it was correct.

If Jensen Huang thinks he can babysit all the AI systems, maybe he should let someone else in on the secret to how to do it? Until then, I'm not sure he's the person I'll be listening to on this subject.

comments.name: LAJ

I designed an expert system back in the1980's. Hardware was much more limited then but the system still had the ability to continually improve itself and based on priorities and results could continuously learn and improve. It was limited to a specific area of expertise and could not learn out side this area. The only reason this was so is because it was bound tightly to the information available ad had no access to the outside world on purpose. People make decisions based on information given to them and emotions. Machines may not have emotions, but the logical conclusion a machine may make is also not based on empathy. You can make a processor or any piece of hardware make different decisions simply by the use of different goals and information. Since society can not fully control the information and goals there is no way to fully control the results. We have already seen this by multiple rogue attacks. Mr. Huang knows this, if he doesn't he should not be one of the heads of the snake.

comments.body: I've never felt passionate about the death penalty either way.  But I have noticed that most of the arguments in favor in the comment sections I've seen in various outlets contain a lot of rage and vindictiveness, and very little genuine contemplation or reason.  That alone makes a strong case against.

comments.name: John Shanley
comments.body: I oppose the death penalty, for a variety of reasons. But if you're going to execute people this way, you can't have incompetent people doing it when legitimate healthcare workers refuse to do it. I don't get the need to put people to death; I'd prefer that to living in a cell for 30+ years. And these cases are called "the state vs. whoever" for a reason; the victim's mom shouldn't get a say in the punishment. Ms. Pike isn't going to be walking the streets endangering the populace. There's no reason to kill her, other than vengence. We should be better than this.

comments.name: Dane B. McFadhen
comments.body: Now should begin her return to a living life. I could see her being educated and then doing work for others in a sealed setting. Anyone, after going through something as horrendous as this, would look at life differently, perhaps reverently.

comments.name: Gil
comments.body:
Christa Pike did more than just savagely murder a person. She also attempted to strangle an inmate with a shoestring, nearly killing her before staff intervened. She was convicted of attempted first-degree murder for that assault.

Her violent behavior inside the prison, also included a later 2012 prison escape plot were motivations for keeping her in isolation. Solitary may seem like cruel and unusual punishment to some -- but how else do you protect the inmate population from a person of this nature? 

Keeping her in shackles in the hospital is a smart move! Based on her behavior, that's not cruel and unusual, it is smart!

comments.name: Lost Sailor
comments.body: I was young but remember all of this well. 1974 was near the end of a period of time marked by political assassinations, when bombings  were common, frustration over segregation, inequality and racism had spawned riots in major cities and young people regularly  battled police on college campuses and in the streets. Most of those taking on the establishment were anti-war or looking for social justice, most were not ultra-left revolutionaries like the SLA.  Now the extremist revolutionary energy has shifted right. There are hundreds of armed ultra-right wing groups, many espousing  civil war.   A key difference -- Our current president shut down the arm of the FBI dedicated to investigating these organizations and pardoned members of right-wing groups every bit as extreme as the SLA , like the Oath Keepers who attempted a violent take over of the federal government.

comments.name: Thomas Radke
comments.body: I entered basic training at Ft. Jackson, SC on Apr15th, 1974. We recruits were pretty much totally isolated from the outside world. No TV, radio or newspapers. The only knowledge of the news we received was through letters from family or friends or through things overhead in our old WWII barracks. My buddy wrote me about the latest antics of this revolutionary group of violent radicals. Something about rumors that they may have plans to attack army training bases. Apparently some truth to this existed as all of a sudden we were starting to get assigned shifts walking guard duty around the area armed with nothing more deadly that a 6" length of pipe used to join the 4 legs of stacked bunks. Hardly a battle worthy weapon. Eventually this threat faded, these miscreants were arrested and military life moved on. I ended up stationed in West Germany where we American soldiers were being threatened by the Red Army Faction and the Baader–Meinhof Group.

comments.name: Not dere no mo

comments.name: Julia
comments.body: I have watched these, and sucked in by the cliffhanger, even subscribed (before cutting myself off after a week). The article raises some interesting points and highlights a few of the deficits but you could go so much deeper into it. Where to start. 1. Let's not be so dismissive of the audience. I read widely and voraciously, I have a BA in English Lit from a highly regarded university, I am in my mid 40s and I also like A24, the Criterion Collection, the Booker Prize novels and A+ serialized dramas and I even have friends IRL but the reality is I am mostly short on time when it comes to consuming 1-2 hours of television. I do not prioritize watching television daily as some people do.  2. *Most* of what is produced is bad, but some is very compelling. When it is satisfying, it is highly satisfying. It's just so hard to find a really great one 3. AI: It's here, it's def got its kinks (pronunciation, some audio artificiality) but honestly it's not that much worse than bad acting + bad script and the quality of AI improves at lightspeed. What AI can do in terms of the quality of the light, the variety of the camera angles and special effects is often incredible, especially in the omegaverse/ high fantasy genre. This is already impacting Hollywood, isn't it? I was initially excited to see a lengthy article on verticals, a little less excited after I read this hot take, characterizing it as the downfall of humanity and the dregs of an art that is fundamentally about escapism.

comments.name: Kate
comments.body: I generally try to avoid  synthetics, partly just because I like the look and feel of natural fibers better and partly for environmental reasons. It's not that I worry too much about my own health from wearing synthetics; frankly, I think people get a little hysterical about it. The much greater concern is the microplastics that shed when polyester clothes are washed. They are too small to be filtered out in municipal water filtration systems, so they get into the water and from there into plants and animals (including those we eat), as well as our drinking water.  I read somewhere that we all have about the same amount of plastic in our bodies that is in a credit card. We don''t really know how harmful it is, but contaminating the planet with our plastic waste has got to be bad.

comments.name: Bruce
comments.body:
Sometimes the effects of technology on the environment become apparent suddenly and change comes quickly after an eye opening event like Three Mile Island had on Nuclear energy. Sometimes things drag on for years like the climate crisis and petroleum use. People don't want to change once they have found products to be useful if they can convince themselves it's not that bad. This is the reason the EPA was founded. To check new products for safety and to clamp down on products that have deadly consequences. But the EPA was always a pipe dream in a country built on Capitalism and it seems to have no agency at all to effect safety in the Citizens United era.
There maybe is no specific disease of micro or nano plastic particles that one could point to that might ignite a 3MI moment for the severe restriction of plastic but consider this, especially if you subscribe to a MAHA outlook. Plastic and the vast array of chemicals used to make it and give it various properties are known to cause human reproductive and endocrine disruption and a host of other health issues like inflammation. Why vaccines as cause for autism when parents and grandparents give their children millions of tons of plastic toys, impregnated with chemicals, that babies and young children then suck on, chew and expose themselves to daily? Does your baby suck on a plastic pacifier? Let's restrict plastic production and find safe alternatives for everything made of plastic, especially toys and clothes. It's time.

comments.name: Voilacestmoi
comments.body: Maybe I read it too quickly but this article seems to be missing the main quality issues with most polyester clothing items and other synthetic fabric. The pill, break, and smell. Any athlete or even occasional gym-goer knows the difference between trying to keep a cotton shirt smelling good and a synthetic one, even after the wash. Of course there are plenty of low-quality cotton goods (quality has dropped across the board), but it’s usually a better bet. For sustainability I try to only get recycled polyester when I do buy it but the pilling can be even worse with those items due to shorter fibers.

comments.name: KarenAnn
comments.body:
My friends used to call me a fabric snob because I was always checking the fiber content of clothing.   I learned about fabrics from a great aunt in the 1950s and 60s who schooled me on what good fabric was.   Natural fibers last longer and can be repaired either through darning or  needle weaving if need be.   But, I find that the fabric weight of today's wools, cottons and linens are different that 50-60 years ago, thinner, not as robust.   
A young woman I know (in her 20s) scours thrift stores for natural fiber vintage clothing, especially the wools.   She uses the fabrics to make her own clothing.

comments.name: trebor
comments.body: "Influencers" who try on clothes as their claim to fame. What does that say about our culture? It's not good.

comments.name: AA20
comments.body: I wish there was more discussion about government regulation of these harmful chemicals. It shouldn't be up to the individual to protect themselves. I just finished reading "They Poisoned the World, Life and Death in the Age of Forever Chemicals," and it was a reminder of how much power corporations have over pollution from by-products during production.

comments.name: M
comments.body:
As someone who prefers synthetic fabrics (not the cheap stuff, but mid-higher end stuff like Outlier, Lululemon, etc.) maybe this will mean lower prices for me. I have noticed a fair amount of concern and discourse about this for years among the more fashoin focused people, though I'm curious how they (most are stridently left wing) will adapt if avoiding plastics becomes MAGA/Right-wing coded. 

Of course I want to be as healthy as possible but in some cases the benefits of synthetic are so much that I'd be willing to accept some amount of risk. Also I appreciate the design and experimentation that goes in to many synthetic garments vs. boring old natural that has been the same for years. For example, I find that I use the extra pocket Lululemon adds to their ABC pant so much that I consider it essential for daily casual wear, I have yet to find a company that offers designs like that in cotton clothing.

comments.name: Ter
comments.body:
Having nothing to do with science it’s been years since I’ve been  able to wear anything but cotton next to my skin. It may not be allergy but synthetics cause my skin to itch.  

A few years ago I was taking a few medications which  side effects included skin sensitivity and most clothes bothered my skin. Thankfully I stopped that medication.

comments.name: Kevin Cahill
comments.body: We need better relations with Russia, China, Iran, and all nations more than we need more ships.  Ships are sitting ducks in a drone war.

comments.name: JBF
comments.body: After China, the second and third largest shipbuilding countries are US allies Korea and Japan, which I can attest are world class in size and efficiency. Why not build there, where US Navy repairs are already allowed? The Trump administration recently tried to get a waiver for a few ships per class of ship to be be built in Korean and Japanese yards, but Congress has stripped most of this request. We should supplement subsidizing US yards with relying on existing allied infrastructure, rather than succumbing to parochial interests which have resulted in a terrible domestic ability to build new war fighting ships.

comments.name: KM
comments.body: Excellent piece! Now if only Mr. Trump were more strategically fearful (shipbuilding and chokepoints) and less tactically greedy (AI and crypto), the country’s economy and foreign policy would be far more balanced and resilient! Well…one can always dream!

comments.name: Bruce Berckman
comments.body: Surface vessels seem almost like sitting ducks when you consider the types of anti-ship armaments that the militarily advanced nations like Russia and China possess. From everyday cruise and hypersonic anti-ship missiles to submarine-launched undersea drones to aerial drone swarms and to whatever else armaments they might have that threaten surface vessels, the modern facts of war seem to suggest that for the US to invest heavily in surface vessels could be an unwarranted, even foolish, risking of money, matériel, and naval personnel. Even moderately powerful militaries like Iran and N Korea may soon possess armaments that could sorely threaten surface vessels, even entire carrier strike groups. Surface vessels seem to be becoming almost what tanks have become in ground warfare: things that hold military personnel, are easily spotted, and easily destroyed. Submarines and commercial vessels, fine, but more easy targets, probably not a good idea!

comments.name: RME
comments.body: This is not a new issue. Arguably the Jones Act is an industrial policy that fails to serve its purpose - maintain a reliable US shipbuilding and sea lift capacity. The remedy is also something about which people in the industry mostly agree. Allow foreign carriers to compete in domestic shipping trade. Which would shift a lot of cargo from motor freight to ships, which is good for a variety of reasons. E.g., MARAD 95 suggests much of the long haul cargo on I 95 would move to ships, lowering both shipping and road repair costs. Subsidize mariners and marine trades. Import shipbuilding expertise. E.g., Japan and South Korea build ships dramatically cheaper and faster than the US does with equivalent labor costs. Essentially it would be re-regulating an industry that was deregulated in the 80s. And be careful citing Capt Mahan. He made things up to support his conclusions.

comments.name: GaryV
comments.body:
China is run as a command economy. A few people set the strategy and it is carried out efficiently. The U.S. is a democracy and it is like a huge cruise ship that can only turn very slowly. We cannot have an industrial policy, we can only direct Government funds to encourage or discourage certain parts of our economy.

What I do not understand is why we have to treat China as a competitor and possibly one day as an enemy.

The U.S. has enough problems with enormous wealth inequality, huge debt and other national issues. It is well past time to address them.

comments.name: Edward
comments.body: Utterly inept leadership by the United States has destroyed our world power.  If it wasn't for our nuclear stockpile other countries would laugh in our face.  We are just a well supplied North Korea in the making.

We are seeing this play out in real time both in terms of national security and commerce. Being able to build and service modern sea worthy vessels in a timely manner is essential.  To do so, we must prioritize revitalizing the ship building industry.

comments.name: Sixofone
comments.body:
India is a democracy in the same way that America was before the civil rights legislation of the '60s. That is, it's not a democracy.

With anything other than full adult suffrage, a country's "democracy" is just branding.

comments.name: Anand
comments.body: The claim that the BJP won West Bengal by striking people off the voter list is poor reporting. Indian media analyzed the seat changes and deleted voters and found they could not draw a correlation. It cut both ways. And Bengali Hindus had a strong reason to vote for the BJP: they saw the carnage against Hindus in neighboring Bangladesh. The TMC was being partial towards Muslims and protecting Muslim criminals from arrest by the Central Police by using Bengal Police.

comments.name: Malone
comments.body:
I am an Indian American from West Bengal, where Modi's BJP has worn statewide elections for the first time ever. The article is not complete because it does not mention how crudely Modi and the BJP refer to Indian Muslim citizens. Some time back Modi quoted a hypothetical  Muslim as proudly proclaiming ``We five our twenty five'' - implying that the man had four wives per Islamic law, and each of the wives had five children. That is a lie but that works in getting racist Hindus even more worked up. The newly elected chief minister of West Bengal keeps threatening that he will outlaw ``love jihad'' - a supposed conspiracy by fundamentalist Muslim young men to make Hindu women fall in love with them and marry them after converting to Islam. He also promises to outlaw ``land jihad'' - which is a conspiracy by secret Muslim groups to buy land in Hindu dominated areas to turn them into Muslim majority. As we are seeing in the US, for fascism to be successful it is not required that there be a majority of racists, a substantial fraction can just poison the system enough.
It is because the majority of Indian citizens have noticed this BJP bias for a long time they are willing to believe that the cutting off of people's voting rights was done in illegal biased manner.

comments.name: Parsons
comments.body:
The right wing ethnofascists of the world are clearly playing to win at this point. They believe they have the electoral backing (and financial backing now, thanks to Trump the tech billionaires) to put democracy on the backburner as a concept and have permanent hegemony over the world

Time will tell if they succeed but as of now it's getting harder to claim they don't have the wind at their back at least, especially in Latin America

If there's any solace, Europe will be a lot harder for them to conquer because of the anti-oligarchal EU system running a check against their racketeering corruption and their roughshodding over the rule of law

Not to mention the multiparty parliamentary system is very hard to subvert without an unusual absolute majority amount of seats going the fascists' way in elections. If you wanna protect your democracy the best way is to always start with or change to one that is NOT a purely presidential system

comments.name: malik
comments.body: With roughly 20–25% of Indians lacking a birth certificate, millions of adults must rely on alternative documents, like school records and voter IDs, to prove their identity. Deletion from the voters' list therefore impacts far more than just elections; it disrupts access to healthcare, education, and legal protection. Marginalized communities, including Muslims, Christians, and Dalits, often face the highest hurdles due to these systemic documentation gaps.

comments.name: John Walker
comments.body: With so many predictions of the decline of democracy, it's good to know that there are millions who insist on their right to vote.

comments.name: ALM
comments.body:
India has had a very unreliable system for recording birth, death, and marriage certificates. I am 90 years old and do not possess a birth certificate. My three siblings also lacked birth certificates. My parents, both grandfathers and grandmothers, many uncles, and aunts similarly did not have birth certificates. Consequently, on paper, they were not recognized as Indian citizens. My siblings, parents, uncles, aunts, and grandparents are all deceased. They were all born, lived, and died in India. Unfortunately, I have no living relatives who can certify that I was born in India. 

There must be millions of Indians, across all religions, who are "stateless" on paper. It is unfair to blame the Modi government or the Election Commission for a problem that has existed for centuries. It is also unjust to accuse the BJP of manipulating voter eligibility. The Election Commission relies on the information available to it.

comments.name: Rita G
comments.body: This is vote rigging, plain and simple.  And if the Indian public still doesn't wake up then there will be no more democracy in India.  Its ironic that its only the young people, the Gen Z, who can see through the eyewash and have the courage to protest.  However its abhorrent to see the sexual assault of female protestors by the police themselves.  Everybody needs to condemn that in the loudest voice.  Don't be distracted by why and why not this SIR exercise should occur.  Free and Fair Elections are the cornerstone of every democracy.  The government can't pick and choose who can vote.

Where there is a will, there is way! and those security guards that stand near emergency door, they do nothing when someone goes in withpout paying. End that program

comments.name: scott
comments.body:
Fare evasion is one of those things that if some get away without paying then it encourages others to also evade.  It creates a mentality of being a sucker if being the person paying when there is no requirement to pay.

When 40% or even 10% are evading fares then security guards enforcing the paying of fares should quickly pay for themselves in fines and reducing fare evasion.  If there were holding cells where fare evaders sat while they were checked for any outstanding warrants then that would significantly raise the cost to fare evaders.

And buses probably would operate better in areas busy enough needing to allow loading in the rear doors.  Collecting fares takes time and has overhead costs.

comments.name: Edward
comments.body: I like these new fare doors; they are the ones I see in Europe, but NYC makes them enter and exit doors, which I hate. In Paris, for instance, they are only for entry, and others are for exit only. Also, when I was visiting Japan, I used the bus, and there you pay when you exit the bus; you can enter for free but can't leave till you pay. I would love to see that here, but it’s culturally unrealistic. Also, while I was in Montpellier, France, their new trolley system is free for the inhabitants with a special pass you apply for; everyone else pays by using an App for their phone or buying a pass. More innovation.

comments.name: Tinmanic
comments.body: Why did the pandemic cause a surge in fare beating, and why did it persist afterward?

comments.name: ppl
comments.body: We have these in Philadelphia at some stations. While I cannot speak to their efficacy in reducing fare evasion, I will say I find it infuriating when someone walks closely behind me to enter the gate on my fare. Before these gates, I felt like fare evaders were cheating the whole system when jumping turnstyles. Obviously, that was a not a good thing. Now, I feel like they are also stealing from me personally by using my fare to enter. I often want to turn around and ask them to pay half, but these days you don't know who you are dealing with so I stay quiet and seethe.

comments.body: Yet here in Seattle, the debate is still ongoing about fare gates because some people consider them to be "unfair" to a certain segment of society.  Mind you, means-tested transit cards are already available, yet not having gates has somehow become a political issue.

I realize there is a considerable difference in scale, but Miami Beach determined that free public transportation paid for itself through sales tax revenue and enormously reduced overhead. It's worth looking into.

I had a corporate black car account in Manhattan and a car in the garage. I used the subway because it was faster. MUCH faster.

comments.name: joe
comments.body: the governor is wrong about what's "more frustrating" - as a paying rider, i personally care way more about how soon the next train is coming than whether some other person jumped the gate. been seeing 10-minute headways on the f line during rush hour, and that's just nonsense.

So many online accounts, particularly financial, in essence require an app, or at least ability to receive a code.  I finally gave in. I haven't had a full-blown phone obsession come about, and I still do no social media.  My family finds it easier to reach me.  Seems like these things can be handled with moderation instead of extremities.  But the things are now almost impossible to avoid, for the reason I have stated. Having one has now made my life easier, not having to surmount that hurdle every day of not having one and having access made difficult because of that.

comments.name: E Plurbis Unum
comments.body:
A couple questions about this.

The only news I had of the outbreak was a clip of a major news outlet (sorry, I am unsure which but maybe CBS) stating the following:

The outbreak at a presumed Russian bioweapons lab in Siberia, naming the victim, the apparent lockdown on information, and the following information:  

200 possible contacts were under quarantine.  

They also discussed the number of scheduled airline flights out of the city, but without stating if ant contacts were on those flights.

That item did not identify the organism, but did use the more specific term “Pneumonic Plague”, which presumably means Yersinia Pestis, cause of the Black Plague of the middle ages transmitted by fleas borne by rodents but also close exposure to
the pneumonic form.

Which can kill in 24-48 hours, but has a far lower rate of transmission than measles or Omicron in people not forced to rely on shared body heat to survive.

Plague is treatable with antibiotics, but by the time someone is diagnosed with pneumonic plague, the next stop is the morgue.

I was unaware of a vaccine, but it is listed on the CDC web site, as mostly needed by those at exposure risk, but a statement that it was unknown if it would prevent pneumonic plague following aerosol exposure.  

Looks like the answer is NO.

Containment should not be difficult, with two caveats:

1.  The Russian authorities are being completely opaque about this.

2.  We do not know if the Russian created more contagious variant.
