comments.name: Kahindo
comments.body:
Globally, ocean fish stocks are not collapsing across the board.  Most fish caught today come from sustainable stocks, but one-third of all stocks are overfished.

The North Pacific Fishery Management Council and Alaska Department of Fish & Game operate one of the world’s most conservative quota systems. Pollock fisheries across the Bering Sea, Aleutians, and Gulf of Alaska are operating under bycatch-controlled quotas and remain open with no overfishing signals.   Pacific cod, sablefish, and multiple rockfish species are also operating under bycatch regulated cooperative programs, indicating stable biomass and controlled harvest.  Crab stocks are more variable and respond strongly to environmental conditions.

Why then are salmon in such a decline?  Salmon depend on both rivers and the ocean and nearly every part of their life cycle is being disrupted. Stressors hit salmon at every stage, but CLIMATE CHANGE is the big one.

Freshwater impacts:
Warmer rivers reduce oxygen and cause direct mortality.
Reduced snowpack → lower summer flows → warmer water.
Altered precipitation → more floods and droughts that destroy redds (nests).

Ocean impacts:
Marine heatwaves disrupt food webs and reduce prey availability.
Ocean acidification harms plankton and shellfish that salmon feed on.
Shifting currents alter migration routes and timing.

These ocean changes explain why even pristine Alaskan rivers can have collapsing salmon runs: the problem is often in the ocean, not the river.

comments.name: scott
comments.body:
The problems that can be addressed is the overfishing from the trawlers and foreign vessels.  The salmon fishery on the much further south Klamath River is rapidly recovering after the removal of dams so it is hard to argue that climate change is the main issue.  A stressed fishery should have ample resources to protect against illegal fishing and should have strict rules preventing bycatch.

It really isn't Alaska's responsibility to stop producing oil and gas as there is strong demand.  Addressing the demand side would be far more effective at reducing consumption.  Trying to artificially make something scarce rarely works.

comments.name: Mary Sweeney
comments.body:
I'm 70 years old. Back when I was in junior high we were assigned reading material and had discussions about the virtually limitless resources of the oceans and how they were easily going to feed Earth's growing population. We also were taught about the greenhouse effect caused by adding carbon to the atmosphere. But these subjects were taught separately with no discussion of their interaction. Oops. 

My junior high days are long gone. Now, in  2026, there is no defensible excuse for overlooking the effects of climate change. Regulating the amount of fishing will help for a while but in the end the industry will still be devastated if we continue to pretend that climate change is no big deal.

comments.name: Christopher
comments.body:
It should surprise no one that neither candidate for Alaska’s Senate seat is speaking clearly about the responsibility of human-caused climate change for the collapse of fish populations. Trawling, whether by ships from China, Russia or Seattle clearly needs to be stopped to stanch the bleeding, but even the strictest ban is unlikely to do more than buy a little time while warming rivers and oceans wipe out salmon fishing altogether.

This issue neatly illustrates why the u.S. Senate needs to be abolished. Unrecognized in this article is how the failure to adequately restrict the destructive effects of extractive industries like oil and fishing is baked into the political over-representation of low population states where such industries dominate both economic and political life in the highly undemocratic body known as the U.S. Senate. 

The majority of Americans live in nine states represented by a total of 18 U.S. Senators, the same number who represent the nine least populous states (including Alaska) that account for 2.4% of the population of the U.S. but where oil, gas, fishing, timber and mining companies effectively own their congressional delegations. Throw in another ten rural but slightly more populous states where giant agribusiness companies exercise a similar death grip on political power and you can use the threat of a filibuster to kill any bill in the Senate you please. Long before Citizens United this imbalance ensured the rule of the of the super-rich.

In 1947, Parke-Davis researchers isolated Chloromycetin—now called chloramphenicol—from cultures of Streptomyces venezuelae and established that it worked as an antibiotic. My late father Quentin R. Bartz authored a paper describing its isolation and purification. 

But a challenge arose when chemists tried to build the molecule in the laboratory. Its atoms can occupy four different three-dimensional arrangements, or stereoisomers. The therapeutically active arrangement is called D-threo, matching the natural antibiotic. The synthesis therefore required separating out the correct form—a process chemists call resolution, often performed on an intermediate before completing the molecule. Parke-Davis’s 1949 synthesis work explicitly describes that step. 

So more than 75 years ago, similar work was being done  -- successfully.

My partner, who has a more traditional "suburban" idea of what a yard should look like, had been bothering me about our formerly pristine goldfish & reflection pond, as I've encouraged it to become "overgrown and messy" with a wide array of native plants (bog bean, pickerel weed, native pond lilies, Joe Pie weed, native monarda, etc.) But we both agree: the wild life transformation is incredible! After only a few years it is filled with salamanders and efts, 4 different kinds of frogs, dragonflies, migratory wood ducks, a cornucopia of egg masses and tadpoles in the spring, and a variety of visiting birds, bear and deer. New England has been affected by alternating drought and flooding, so small ponds also serve an ecological purpose in both situations.

comments.name: Doogster

I dug a pond in our back yard where rainwater had been pooling.  It would be too difficult to dig for a storm drain.  This pond has been a ecological success!  It has been here for four seasons and this year was the best.

We had five Eastern Spotted Newts.  At the beginning of the season we had as many as 50 male Wood Frogs and over 35 egg masses.  One day I heard a major chorus in the pond.  The Woodies were having a "pool party"!  They were jumping in and out of the pond.  I actually observed a number of Woodies jump up in the air and land flat on their backs on some pond plants.  We now also have two Green Frogs that have taken up residence in a container next to the pond.  They come up out of the water and perch on the edge of the container watching us.  They've been there of over two months.

This has been the best season yet.

"Sprawl" is the term for everything in Hunterdon County and especially all the suburbaness that has oozed into its County Seat, Flemington,from places like Hillsborough, New Jersey. One doctor (a native a Brooklyn) told me:"I never left Brooklyn to substitute living in an ugly eyesore of suburbia like Hillsborough."

comments.name: RC

I do have a small filter which I clean periodically to limit algae growth, but main issue is the local fauna that invade my pond.  Deer eat my water lily. Fox, bear,and raccoons eat my fish(having started out small feeder goldfish) and growing up for years.  I have been forced to create a chicken wire “cover” to keep them out.  Somehow frogs disappear and reappear each year.  I still enjoy it, but it is not maintenance free by any stretch.

comments.name: Lilly Guerrero
comments.body: I feel like it takes me a long time to get started on things and it just feels like a drag and makes me feel unmotivated. If it’s something that doesn’t interest me or something that I want to do then I tend to not want to do it so I push it back to the last minute. I want to change that because it only causes more assignments for me to do and it’s just a big pile of stuff that i need to get at the same time. The same with my room. I tend to not pick up as often as I should because I don’t like being in there unless i’m sleeping or getting clothes so because i’m not in there a lot it doesn’t interest me to pick it up. I want to change those habits but old habits die hard so hopefully little by little it could change.

comments.name: Jonah S.
comments.body: I’m a procrastinator but in a weird way. Half of the time I’ll do all the work the second I get it. Other times I wait, then I wait some more, wait again, and then Thursday night I do all my homework. It is kind of a weird thing to do because it's like polar opposites. I personally don’t come up with an excuse, I just say to myself I’ll do it later, and that later being four days. If it’s something really big I will try to get it done quickly just because I know it takes more than 2 hours or so. The one exception for me is I will almost always find a time where I finish all the work, and then just do my homework in school. Other times I’m allowed to do my homework in the class. For me the main thing that stops me from doing all of my homework sooner is just a mix of laziness, and honestly it’s just not enjoyable. I am someone that loves to learn in lots of different ways. Homework is not one of them. For me homework is just a pain. Why should I have to do work once I finish school? That's what I tell myself at least. Sometimes the homework is really enjoyable for me. I will procrastinate on assignments that I don’t like, but assignments that I enjoy (projects) I will always get done pretty fast. That is the main reason why I procrastinate. I honestly just don’t enjoy doing a lot of the assignments, but every once in a while I will get that one fun project. However, some projects can be really bad and boring. I’ll usually procrastinate on those, but that's why I procrastinate.

comments.name: Umar S
comments.body: Procrastination is a dangerous thing that many students do—including me. I usually procrastinate to do homework or study—especially after a long day of school. Procrastination affects me because I have to cram more studying in a shorter amount of time, leading to worse scores. People against procrastination would certainly take issue with the argument that because we are lazy, we procrastinate. However, do they think about the times that we come home exhausted, hungry, and think about school as the last thing? Maybe we procrastinate because we want some rest from all of the commitments we have every week. I know that procrastination is bad, so don't do it.

comments.name: Avi George
comments.body: Doom scrolling. That's all I want to do when I get home from a long day of school, then, I see a project due. Then stress kicks in. Finishing the project becomes my first priority. I finish my project so I can get my freetime and receive the feeling of relaxation. Seeing that nothing else is due just makes me feel accomplished.

comments.name: Jane Courtin
comments.body:
"Dear Future Me, 
You have a project due on Friday that involves so much work! What will you be doing on Friday? Should I do this project now? What if you are doing absolutely nothing on Friday? But what if my friend invites me over and I can’t go because of this project?"
I always ask myself this question when I am assigned something. I am not a procrastinator, not at all. Once I get assigned something, I will sit at my desk, get comfy, put on music, and do everything on my agenda. As a person whose calendar is spilling from the glass and barely has free time, it is very important to get all my stuff done early so I have time to just decompress and relax. I am always looking forward to Friday because all my work will be done and completed so I can just hang out with my friends or do something active. To me, being disorganized is like a chocolate chip cookie with only one chocolate chip.

comments.name: Solomon
comments.body: f I had to give myself a rating form 1 to 10 on procrastination it would be 3. It would be a 3 because I like to get things done quickly so I can get more time to do other things. But sometimes I do get procrastinated because when I get home from school my mom always asks me if I have any homework but I usually say no which is a lie. Then she checks my to-do and makes me do my homework. But I want to work on that so I am not doing that in high school. But sometimes I do get procrastinated when I am writing. I get procrastinated on writing because I can't express my thoughts on paper. I do this because I always think to myself “that is a bad idea “.

comments.name: Reagan Westfield
comments.body: I am the biggest procrastinator you will ever meet. Everything is pushed back. Right now I am trying to fix it by making a schedule but you know those never work. It's a lot to handle with soccer, volleyball and school work and still being able to say I am having fun with my life. My next grade is rumored to be hard so I've been drawn to quitting soccer next year but then it's  my favorite sport and I'm getting good at it.  Soccer is everyday. Obviously I'm supposed to practice at home, but also the practices are getting harder most of the time I don't want to go anymore. So at this point procrastination is the only thing I can assure you will  happen in my life.

comments.name: Gianfranco Montalto
comments.body: I am a low level procrastinator as I do not procrastinate until I get something I really do not want to do. At that point I look at the task and am like no no I don't want to and don't do it. Some things I really don't want to do are sorting my computer files and deleting photos I don't want. I will always be like well I could do something else. I think I have a hard time doing those things because they are time consuming and boring to complete as I am lazy at times once I start relaxing and I think oh I need to go do this I end up not doing it. Some of the suggestions mentioned in the article do help as just starting makes me actually do it but some don't. For example the reward one doesnt work because I think or i could do the reward now. So in conclusion I believe that the issue I have is laziness as I really don't want to do time consuming and boring tasks. I have used some of these methods to help with procrastination in the past and will try to do some other methods to help with procrastination.

articles.title: Are You a Procrastinator?
articles.summary: Do you find it hard to get started on tasks? Does the urge to postpone and delay make things harder for you?

Im now under the care of a GIST oncologist and monitored for recurrences for life.

I recovered quickly and felt so much better.

I've talked to many doctors over many years and they only mentioned the procedures they themselves perform (like Ablation or Hysterectomy). UAE is performed by a radiologist.

comments.name: Name withheld but
comments.location: this happened, and I'm still in-court
comments.body:
If you want to have children, and you want to have an operation for fibroids, be VERY careful.  I stated clearly that I wanted to preserve fertility and the Geneva University Hospital in Switzerland (called "HUG") where I was living at the time, performed, for reasons no one will tell me, a "endometrial resection", removing and cauterizing the interior of my uterus.  I didn't learn of this for 9 years, and the entire Swiss judiciary (I sued with lawyer and legal insurance) covered for the Swiss Hospital and French citizen surgeon, by outright lying and claiming their consent form gave the surgeon permission to do this to me.

The U.S. government in Switzerland was not helpful.  I am under a FISA warrant done for political purposes while I was working at the UN in Geneva, which is impossible to address in U.S. court.  There's was in-house U.S. DOJ Prosecutor in the U.S. Embassy in Paris named Puneet Kakkar who is nominally blocking my legal actions in Switzerland and France, and this probably had something to do with it.  I have clear statements from famous surgeons (including the surgeon who invented endometrial resection in Rochester New York) that what was done to me was tantamount to sterilization. It's an uphill battle in Switzerland and France to get justice, while the U.S. government is treating FISA warrant like a blanket immunity tool.

I spent years crying about losing the ability to bear a child, now I want to be paid-out and the U.S. government is obstructing that.

comments.name: R Mitchell
comments.body: In 1970, I was an American college student studying in Britain. A classmate and I, on a whim, traveled to Edinburgh and took a morning train to St. Andrews. It was the site of that year's British Open. We walked onto the course -- no fee, no reservation, no one checking credentials -- and stood a few feet away from some of the golf legends of that time. We were amazed that people could play on such a rugged landscape. I have never played golf  myself, but the memory of that day is still strong.

comments.name: Mark A Michelson
comments.body:
The article, the golf and the town are all interesting.  But there is an unfortunate omission.  St. Andrews University is also in the town.  Parts of it are close enough to have a good view of the  golf courses.  The University is also quite old and very highly regarded -- indeed it is quite popular with Americans.
   Because I am lucky enough to have a daughter who is a professor at the University I have visited St. Andrews (and her husband and my grandchildren) repeatedly and enjoyed every visit.
   Mark  A.  Michelson

comments.name: Greg

Our generation that grew up with access to mostly naturally occurring plants had far less overdoses than this current generation.  

This generation grew up with the mentality that pharmaceuticals produced by man can solve problems especially our youth has resulted in far more problems than acknowledged.  In other words they grew up eating Xanax and anti depressants that had far more long term downsides than getting one's hands on cocaine, heroin and marijuana.

Once society cracked down on actual pills that is when people started filling that void with things that would kill this generation, while those that continued to avoid pills did far better over time than this generation.

Our Boomer cohort used all kinds of drugs with far less deaths or long term negative outcomes than this generation.  What we need in society is an honest approach to studying the naturally occurring plants can do for a human and when that use should be encouraged as the pills that man has made are not scrutinized enough to determine the negative outcomes.

comments.name: David Conway
comments.body: The fabric of the town is RAPIDLY fraying  because of the influx of wealthy people who have moved to town in recent years to live full time, or those  who have bought homes as second home/rental properties,  are not part of the COMMUNITY. Where there was once a reasonable level of economic diversity, which created a rich experience, particularly for kids in the school system. Stowe is becoming populated by wealthier people, and home prices are out of reach for most young families- prices have always been higher than those of surrounding towns, but now the prices are  make buying a home out of reach for most families with young children. These new homeowners cannot be bothered to volunteer, to understand what makes the a small rural school system great in ways that cannot be matched by large suburban systems, mainly because the community WAS willing to pay for it. Many of the wealthy families that can afford to move to town care only about their kid, not all of the kids. When their “very special and unique child” says that they are bored one day, instead of having conversations with teachers and principles, they quickly decide to send the kids to private schools or home school. These people are then less likely to vote for a school budget that keeps the schools running at the same level of quality, OR perhaps make improvements where necessary. If you are not exposed, and share experiences of every day life with people that are of lower economic means, than you are less likely to understand their strengths and their needs. Many of these people DO NOT VOLUNTEER.  Yup, I believe that the wealthy are generally more selfish, when they are not sharing experiences with people who do not have the same financial resources and don’t have a common set of goals. Not great for a community that once thrived on a citizenry that once thrived in every way, because of its diversity.

comments.name: MARC WOLFF
comments.body: Stowe is magical. There is no other place like it. Yes the skiing is more consistent out west. But, it can be very good in Stowe too (No altitude acclamation necessary). The people are awesome.. and that’s what it’s really about. The “feel” is very different.  You walk / run and people say Hi..they wave..(they don’t lay on their horns!)  the surrounding towns are even better when it comes to that.. Real genuine caring selflessness everywhere. As far as beauty goes, it’s idyllic.  4 Seasons and your head is constantly on a swivel. It’s THAT PRETTY.  Everything is a picture.  Barely any traffic lights or strip malls or concrete jungles .. or fast food chains..  I would pay more any day of the week for a place in the area than I would out west.  The issue like any awesome place is the secret is out.. started during Covid!

comments.name: Sitges
comments.body:
Sanchez will now pay for the lack of legislation to protect honest homeowners from squatters, aka in Spain as Okupas.  My  sister rented, on a 5 year lease, her  large home in Lloret de Mar to a large Russian family  of 12 members for $1,000 month, way below market value "because they seemed nice and were all working".  In less than a year they stopped paying rent but had continued excuses and promises.  She initiated eviction proceedings 3 years ago which is costly and the process takes at least two years.  Tired of waiting at the inefficiency of the process, her attorney referred to a company of "Desokupas" who within 2 weeks got the squatters to move out , installed  security cameras, new locks on doors and  windos, sent a cleaning agency to scrub and disinfect the  unlivable premises  and the garden that had grown into a jungle.  It cost her close to 10,000 Euros plus the loss of 4 years rent, plus the cost of utilities that renters stopped paying.   She is now in contract to sell the property.  
A first cousin in Barcelona rented the apartment left vacant when her father passed way to a Russian with Argentinian passport, again for 5 years. Shortly, she saw her apartment advertised on Airbnb which is illegal.   Lack of space does not allow me to go into the saga but   City Hall held her responsible for an illegal tourist apartment although she had filed a complaint with them against her tenant.  She's set to go to trial next month to defend herself.  Totally Kafkiest!

comments.name: Jason
comments.body: And make no mistake he will mobilize the left. Property speculation has reached untenable heights and the rightwing coalitions governing the Autonomous Communities (especially Madrid, Valencia, abd Andalusia)—-which manage housing policies—have only added fuel to the fire. They’ve also mostly badly, even criminally, botched management of other crises (wildfires, floods, public healthcare abd education investment) and been caught in corruption scandals that make the Socialists’s look like child’s play. Unbuilt lots—subject to out of control speculation—need to be expropriated for public housing on a large scale. Everyone knows the market has failed and will fail to build on the needed scale—failed everywhere, not only in Spain. Vienna is the model. Everyone in Spain knows this, even PP and Vox supporters. If the left of the left parties put aside their squabbling and present a unified candidacy to complement the Socialists (signs are encouraging that they’ve got finally the fear of God in them) Sanchez could win on the public housing, health care and education platform. I will certainly vote for the left of the left if they unite and otherwise for Sanchez—my first time if it comes to that. But the ultraright destroy everything they touch everywhere—as we’ve seen with Trump’s failed promises on every front.

comments.name: MuggedByReality
comments.body: I think Spaniards have had enough of their double-speak prime minister. Sanchez has been in power for more than 8 years and during that time neither he nor his party made housing a priority. The Tenants’ Unions of Catalonia called Sanchez's latest housing proposals "a farce." Add to that his dismal response to the invasion of Ceuta, he almost certainly is heading toward defeat. Playing savior to cash-strapped Spaniards while his own advisors and family rake in money from government corruption isn't going to cut it. By the end of November he will be out of a job.

comments.name: Plebeianmensch

Spaniards would be foolish to give up all these gains and revert back to a path of regression as the U.S. has been going through under Donald Trump. comments.name: James

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: At the time of the American revolution nobody across Europe ever envisioned that the eventual United States would overtake their empires and become a military, economic, and cultural superpower, effectively dictating the terms of international affairs.  What I see is a country, long exploited and murderously, destructively beat down by the western empires, rising to a position of power and effectively turning the tables on those powers that had been their oppressors.  "What goes around comes around?"  We rightly condemn the brutal repressions of the Communist dictatorship--while largely giving ourselves a pass on those perpetrated by our own government against segments of our own population, indigenous and "imported," as well as all of our country's brutal military, political, and economic interventions especially across Asia, Southeast Asia, Central and South America.  Now the US and European peoples are beginning to experience the first pains of being on the other side of power equation.  Eventually the Chinese people may demand political reforms.  That's my bit of historical perspective.  (Of course humanity now has the capacity to pretty much destroy itself so there is that.)  Sigh...what will today's news hurl at us?

comments.name: James Liu
comments.body: China has leveraged its population to produce exports at lower wages.  Its government provides large targeted subsidies to heavy industry, computing, and solar industries.   It steals technology from Western companies that sell to China by forcing them to share technology in their manufacturing plants in China.  This is why China has excelled in its export production.  Sealing off these avenues may already come too late for some EU industries.  The only way to combat these China advantages is to restrict imports with tariffs and quotas; provide government support to rapidly develop new technologies (i.e. chips act) that are proprietary without giving away the secrets.  This is a long haul strategy and will not solve the trade imbalance overnight.

These places can be hardened.  What can't be safegarded is the multitudes of easily manipulated humans' opinions that AI can very efficiently affect.

comments.name: StopTheSlop
comments.body:
I appreciate the vast complexities involved with LLMs (I refuse to use AI, or the dumber SI, nominative), but at their core, they are hyperadvanced pattern recognition and matching machines. No matter how lifelike the conversation they make, how clean the code they write, how accurate the math equations they solve, they aren't "thinking", they are extrapolating from mountains of data.

If you leave an LLM on its own, with no prompts or inputs, does it do anything? Does it get bored and create it's own stories or art? Or does it just sit, endlessly waiting for a command?

The current LLM models could be used to the great detriment of humanity via cyberattacks and potentially much worse if military integrations continue, but it will be humans dictating the destruction, not the machines.

comments.name: John
comments.body: Nuclear reactors deliver 24/7 baseload electricity, running at about a 93% capacity factor in the US, which is nearly three times that of wind (34%) or solar (23%). They do it on a small footprint: about 1.3 square miles per 1,000 MW, some 27–50 times less land per unit of electricity than coal and ~34 times less than solar PV. Life-cycle emissions are about 12 g CO₂/kWh versus over 800 g for coal. Yet opposition has long been stoked by fossil-fuel interests, from 1970s oil-money grants to anti-nuclear groups to the American Petroleum Institute's campaign against Ohio nuclear support.  Crucially, license renewal, uprating, and refurbishment of the existing fleet sidesteps the high capital cost of new construction, delivering carbon-free power at a fraction of greenfield expense.

If she were asking about her daughter it would be a different story.
Let’s deal with what we know.

I would mount the rug to a long strip of sturdy wood on the back of the rug and then hang the wood. This is how I do tapestries. Tapestries are light so I mount the rough side of velcro to the flat piece of wood like a yard stick. Then I hang the stick and press the tapestry on. No holes in the fabric that way.

I can understand the desperation of the deceased. However this case raises questions about our understanding of the strain causing this outbreak versus the West African outbreak. Upon boarding his flight in Uganda, he seemed to have a normal temperature check allowing him to proceed. This suggests that either the thermometers or the thermal scanning process failed or that fever/high temp is not a useful or reliable indicator. So what is? 

For someone to be ill for a month and die within two days of arrival in Nairobi suggests a different kind of disease progression. 

Or perhaps he bribed someone at the airport just as he probably did in Congo to get across the border. Someone at the airport is probably not expecting a sick Kenyan to have Ebola. 

Food for thought

We need stronger policies and a hard handed government public intervention and institutions when it comes to highly contagious diseases.  The Covid pandemic brought righted winged anger  over Fauci prioritizing public health over individual liberties and our administrations single handed dismantling US aid - We have opened the floodgates to diseases curbing human populations before AI can.  We need to look strongly at these countries not see what we will look like if we don’t reverse what has been undone. comments.name: KPMD
comments.body:
Recent reporting on Kenya’s first confirmed Ebola case highlights glaring oversights regarding screening and security gaps at the departure airport and the airline protocols that allowed a symptomatic passenger to board.

However, looking past the logistical breakdowns, this tragic event is fundamentally about a human being driven to desperation. The individual crossed quietly into Uganda and masked his symptoms to secure better treatment in Kenya. Yet the bitter irony is profound: most hospitals in Kenya are not uniquely structured or equipped to manage a viral hemorrhagic fever of this scale—which is why a specialized unit was established. Had this person sought proper care at an established treatment unit within the eastern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo, he would likely be alive today.

Finally, public health commentary must do a better job of calming public anxiety by emphasizing the facts of transmission. Ebola is not COVID-19; it is not airborne. It cannot be contracted by simply sharing airspace or breathing the same air in a public place. Transmission requires direct physical contact involving the exchange of infectious bodily fluids.

In short, Ebola is not floating around waiting for anyone to catch it. While strict contact tracing and vigilance are essential, letting panic be driven by misconceptions about how the virus spreads only fuels unnecessary fear and pushes vulnerable patients further into the shadows.

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: Cultivating ties with rich donors is literally one of the main jobs of a US university president.  And while rich donors aren't all saints, using that money for higher education is one of the best things we can do as a society.  From what I've heard from alums, Botstein was widely respected for his vision and leadership and it seems like such a waste to force him to resign because of what we know about Epstein now.

comments.name: Borderlands
comments.body:
I attended Bard College for a couple of years decades ago and have had the feeling from the beginning of this sad episode that there were motivations among the trustees and other players with respect to Professor Botstein that had nothing to do with Jeffrey Epstein. Leon Botstein is genuinely one of the smartest non-scientist people you will ever meet and not predisposed in his personality to suffer fools or obstacles with grace. He has mellowed, but it is easy to imagine a lot of long-standing ruffled feathers.

Anyone who does not think that Leon's disposition toward Jeffrey Epstein was not entirely explained by the prospect of a large donation is either an irrational culture warrior or is simply unaware of his decades-long history with an institution constantly on the brink of either having to completely change its character or simply go out of business. There is probably no other college in America whose development and ongoing existence was for decades so reliant on the work of one person. Even ten years ago the idea of feeding him to the outrage machine over something as amorphous as this would have been not so much unthinkable as simply impossible for the college to even consider.

But hat picture changed radically with the Soros gift, and it is not hard to imagine Leon's indispensability coming in for revision over the past few years in its wake. Is it really a coincidence that this all happened immediately after the Soros gift was finalized in January?

comments.name: AW
comments.body: For heaven's sake leave the man alone. He was hounded out of his job and just wants to continue to bring his talents to the music programs and orchestras he founded. His contributions  have been enormous both to Bard and to the arts in general. He has committed no crime. The self-righteous crowd that insists that anyone who doesn't meet their purity tests must be cancelled is sickening. Enough already.

comments.name: David
comments.body: This summer I saw RIchard Strauss's seldom performed opera, "The Egyptian Helen," at the Fisher Center on Bard College.  Leon Botstein picked it (as he determined all past summer season selections), gathered the creative team, and conducted the orchestra.  What can I say?  it was one of the best experiences in the opera of my life - and I've seen a lot.  What a wonderful opera that he unearthed from obscurity.  It was brilliantly staged at a level of artistry we associate with the Met and other world-class opera houses - and here it was - deep in Dutchess County.  The audience gave Botstein tepid applause in contrast to the enthusiastic applause for the musicians and singers.  He faced it all down defiantly.  I, for one, am intensely grateful he gave me and us this extraordinary experience.

comments.name: Grandpa
comments.body:
There is no evidence that Botstein's relationship with Epstein was about anything other than raising money for Bard. Yes, he failed to communicate with the Board of Trustees and ignored concerns of some faculty members. He didn't report consulting fees, which he says he donated to the school (something easily verified). He's a famously head-strong guy, but again, I think the evidence shows that he did succeed in raising money for the school and that his relationship with Epstein had nothing to do with Epstein's criminality.

In general, I think there has been a failure to distinguish between Epstein's interest in supporting some good causes and the criminal side of his life. I'm not talking about Epstein's reputation, about which I could not care less. I'm talking about people whose reputations and work have suffered because of associations with Epstein motivated solely by raising money for good work and no evidence of criminal activities. Some of this kind of damage has been done at MIT.

I think there should be articles about those "critics" who see the world only in black and white and who want to tarnish the reputations of anyone who knew Epstein or other offenders.  Life is a complicated thing to negotiate where one often has to make a lot of choices and compromises.

This reminds of the case of Al Franken who was accused of inappropriate contact with women and was forced to resign.  I've heard from a lot of people that his resignation was a major mistake.  Similarly so, Botstein has acknowledged his relationship to Epstein.  He did not aid or abet Epstein.  That he was forced to resign through "guilt by association" I feel is a great mistake.

comments.name: Prakash Nadkarni
comments.body:
"Palata" is a Burmese variant of the South Asian paratha, a layered flatbread (spelled/pronunced almost identically with L replacing R.   
Burma had a large Indian diaspora during British rule. My recently departed mentor/professor in Mumbai came to India as a 9-year-old refugee with his family after the Japanese invasion of Burma in 1942, crossing the Arakan mountains on foot. A polymath and excellent cook, he made several Burmese dishes at home. Interestingly, Burmese cuisine has its own version of the ubiquitous SE Asian fermented fish/shrimp paste, called ngapi- do a Web search.

The hint of sugar used here in the flatbread isn't common in Indian paratha recipes, but should complement rather than clash with the savory accompaniments. Some paratha recipes use ghee instead of oil, while others use a filling between the layers: onion, radish, potato, ground meat, etc. 

It is fascinating to observe Mr, Thway's dedication to his craft in the video.

comments.name: Paula G
comments.body:
I find being a polyglot is weird and it's very much dependent on the location and time. 

I am a polyglot, and I speak 5 languages at a B2-C2 level (FR,NL,DE,FI,EN) and I can manage well in ES and SE. I can 'fake' understand a lot of languages. But maintaining all these languages takes work; Dutch and German are very close, and I can understand and read them, but I cannot actively speak them at the same time. Learning a language has occasionally led me to be mute in another (I used to be a B2 in Spanish, but after learning FI and DE, I tried to speak Spanish and I couldn't even remember how to say how are you?). And languages depend on place; in Spain I can speak Spanish, but I can't keep it up in my everyday life. 

My biggest fascination with how people react to polyglots is that they think we are obsessed with languages. I learned languages and took learning languages seriously when I moved to a new country - but I cannot stress enough how ridiculously dull learning languages is. Especially when you do it four or more times in a row. You sit in language classes  often with very dull people, and usually a teacher's pet who is obsessed with showing off how much they know. You talk about how work/christmas is in "your" country. It gets you ahead, but it's dull. 

I usually self-learn A1-A2 on my own, then go to a class that's above my level, panic and pull myself ahead, and watch series, films, read books to master the languages.

I hope not.  3 years ago I had back surgery.  I have severe Osteoarthritis and it has attacked cartilage everywhere in my body.  A Robotic arm was used to assist the fusing of 5 vertebrae in my lumbar area.  A skilled surgeon led the team in this 12 hour surgery.  At some point I coded for 8 seconds.  No light at the end of a tunnel appeared.
Imagine the stamina this team of OR nurses, anesthesiologist , MD's and all the unnamed others who assisted for 12 hours.  I recovered and all the pain and sciatica was gone.  I am grateful that no AI or full Robotic techniques were relied on.  The human brain, specially a well -trained one, is much more pliable than robotics.  It can respond more quickly with a solution to an unanticipated event and affect a good outcome.  I am grateful to live near the Tucson Medical Center Orthopedic Hospital.  I am very  grateful for all the medical professionals living and practicing here.  The only improvements is to solve the lack of Primary Physicians and increase the research dollars.  Also, TMC is the last of two not-for-profit healthcare providers.  I wish we had Universal Healthcare for all and I would be willing to pay higher taxes to make that happen.

comments.name: Tim
comments.body:
It is often difficult to not view solutions to the challenges in Malawi through a Western lens, especially since issues of this magnitude rarely have simple answers. Having had friends live there for decades and having volunteered in Malawi myself to help locals improve their business skills in the food industry, I have seen firsthand a reality that is hard for many to imagine. A common saying there is, "He that has food is rich."

Education levels remain low, with roughly 60% literacy and only about 8% completing high school. Compensation is extremely minimal—a casual worker earns around $1 a day to support a family—and only about 1% of the population has refrigeration.

Despite these hardships, the people are exceptionally kind. In the local language, Malawi means "warm heart," which aligns entirely with my experience.

Dedication of time, talents, and resources toward helping a nation learn to feed itself and educate its children is a life well spent. Who is ready to step up next?

comments.name: Const
comments.body:
There is a larger story here that deserves attention. South Africa is hardly alone in pushing migrants back across its borders. Iran and Pakistan have carried out mass deportations of Afghans, with hundreds of thousands forced back to a country many had fled, while other countries are also tightening immigration enforcement.

The reality is that when large numbers of people leave poorer or less stable countries seeking work and opportunity, eventually the receiving countries may decide they simply cannot—or will not—absorb them indefinitely. The result is painful for migrants and the families who depend on the money they send home. South Africa's experience is a reminder that migration pressures don't disappear simply because people desperately want to leave home.

The people of Malawi have to reorganize their government and society so that their needs and aspirations can be met. comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
Many people are upset about migration and inflation. However many people are unaware that climate change is an increasing driver of both. By voting for right wing politicians who deny climate science they are working to make climate change impacts worse, driving even more migration and inflation.

Many people think that today’s migrations and high prices are due only to political or economic policy, missing the underlying catalyst: climate change. 

Extreme weather, prolonged droughts, and crop failures are driving global migration as unlivable conditions force millions from their homes. 

Simultaneously, these same climate shocks trigger "climateflation." Scorched agricultural land and collapsing supply chains drive up the cost of everything from food to insurance. 

Connecting these dots shows that migration and inflation are some of the  symptoms of a heating planet.

And the coming refuge flows, as climate change related impacts continue to intensify very nonlinearly, will dwarf those that we've seen so far.

There seems to be a real character problem emerging for Republicans on the ballot this year. In several unexpectedly competitive races, Democrats aren’t just benefiting from dissatisfaction with Trump or the economy, they’re running against Republicans carrying serious personal and ethical baggage, while presenting candidates whose campaigns emphasize decency, faith and public service. Adam Hamilton in Kansas and James Talarico in Texas are obvious examples, and both are running competitively in states Trump won comfortably in 2024. 

What’s especially interesting about Max Miller is the lesson he appears to have taken from the Trump era: when your personal conduct becomes an electoral liability, don’t retreat. Instead, deny, fight and trust partisan loyalty to carry you through. Miller has refused to withdraw while denying the allegations against him, even as members of his own party initially urged him to step aside. 

But 2026 may be testing the limits of that strategy. Voters can disagree profoundly about policy and still care whether the people asking to represent them demonstrate judgment, integrity and basic decency. Maybe character didn’t disappear as an electoral issue after all.

My experience in the faith sounds eerily similar to the author’s. Sometimes on but usually off, it provided comfort and a beautiful routine but little more.  I usually referred to myself as an agnostic. Sometimes I’d call myself an atheist. Then, after a couple brushes with death and feeling just awful for myself, I prayed out for help from the crevices at the bottom of a pit of despair—the last resort of a scoundrel. I was out of reach of any comfort that exists on this world. So, long story short, he showed up! It was really cool. So, as a thank you to The Big Guy, I decided to give faith an honest try for the first time. I’m still terrible as an adherent, as I am at most things, but by this point I’m good enough at it to understand that grace is everywhere all the time. The details of how to see it are still murky to me, but it has something to do with slowing down, opening up, and seeing loving kindness in every persons soul. Not just during sunsets over the Rockies but everywhere. Even here, at McDonald’s while I drink my scalding hot coffee and type out this message.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
Myron Cohen's work has been foundational in the fight against HIV. It was his work that demonstrated that people with undetectable viral loads did not transmit the virus to HIV negative partners. In other words, successful treatment is effective in preventing future infections.

The rapid retrenchment of global HIV treatment and prevention support makes us more vulnerable to an expanding epidemic. Under DOGE, treatment programs and networks in Africa were dismantled for months or longer; due to the pharmacokinetics of antivirals, we have now probably established widespread transmission of treatment-resistant HIV. That means ongoing transmission. We can't establish the scope of the problem because surveillance funds were cut.

It may be that the USG should not have to bear so much of the financial burden of HIV programs in Africa and elsewhere, but as HIV resistance becomes more and more prevalent it will be clear that stopping programs on a dime, without adequate planning beforehand, is neither efficient nor effective.

HIV vaccine trial grant proposals (having failed over 40 years to produce a single effective HIV vaccine) merit review with scrutiny. Perhaps other interventions merit more funding. However, breaking up the networks without adequately supporting the information, care and prevention they provide will likely cost, in lives and dollars, in the long run. 

NYT should report in detail on HHS's future plans.

I work in one of these networks and it is so important to emphasize that what the networks do adapts to needs over time. We are already adapting to the implementation science push that the NIH director is quoted about in this article. We can be nimble and study what is important in different eras, but if our infrastructure is destroyed, that possibility is gone. And the studies already in the pipeline are being delayed indefinitely, which is a huge cost to the people waiting for answers. We responded to mpox urgently and also continue to focus on hepatitis, tuberculosis, and aging and cardiovascular disease with HIV. The existence of some tools doesn’t mean we break the tool shop. It’s also slower and WAY more expensive to do these studies as one-offs than in a streamlined network- so it will just waste taxpayers time and money. If you know anyone impacted by any of these health issues, or are just riled about how much time and money is being squandered by halting mid-project, please let your congressional offices know how important this work is!

comments.name: I Am
comments.body:
Yeah, Serling has been the instigator of many great stories, and he has indeed contributed a lot, but it never is a one man operation.  The people who overall are the ones with the power to help. And as long as people are conditioned to assume fundamental separation between themselves and everything else, there will appear dissatisfaction/suffering. 

Once there is an apparently separate "me" here and a world of "other" over there, there is something that must be protected, defended, completed, validated, compared, maintained, and controlled. What is appearing can then be divided into what "I" want and don't want, what should and shouldn't be happening, what threatens or benefits "me", and what must change before "I" can be okay. 

This doesn't mean distinctions disappear or that nothing matters; distinctions can remain deeply and intimately felt and relatively meaningful without requiring fundamental separation between them. As this conditioning is dissolving here, compassion and empathy appear bottom up, & the unconditional nature of what is appearing is recognized/revealed. 

Our issues can't be solved using the same assumptions that got us to this point.

comments.name: IanC
comments.body: I fall squarely into this category (53M) and look forward to watching this show with my girlfriend (50F).  I find dating at this age so fun and rewarding.  It has taken a while to adjust to not having specific relationship/couple "goals" like marriage, kids, house, etc - we have had all that!  Now we get to focus on ourselves and negotiate what is meaningful for us.  If I may, here are some suggestions I have germane to some of the issues raised in the article:  For the fellas, listen to your dates and don't monologue. Pay attention to your grooming, dress, tone of voice, keep a clean house, perfect a couple recipes for dinner (and later, breakfast, Ooooh-la-la!)  and work on cultivating genuine interest in the person you're with.  I have it on good authority that this is the sexiest thing ever!  For the ladies, as a healthcare provider, I highly recommend discussing hormone replacement therapy with your medical provider.  Especially consider a hormonal IUD if that's right for you.  HRT in general can really elevate your sexy time!
